extracted.intended_audience: general readers (non-Brits) confused about terminology around the U.K./Britain/England, especially in light of Brexit
extracted.subtask_description: A short primer for non-specialist readers explaining the proper geographic and political uses of the terms 'United Kingdom', 'Great Britain' (Britain), 'England', and related designations, plus related categories (Overseas Territories, Crown Dependencies, Commonwealth Realms).

rubrics_metrics.name: United Kingdom (U.K.) = sovereign state of four countries
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.K., as it is called, is a sovereign state that consists of four individual countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'United Kingdom' or 'U.K.' when referring to the sovereign state comprising those four countries. Note that within the U.K. Parliament is sovereign, but the constituent countries have varying degrees of autonomy (see 'reserved' vs 'devolved' matters). Do not use 'England' or 'Britain' when you mean the entire sovereign state if that would exclude Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great Britain (Britain) = the island containing England, Scotland, Wales
rubrics_metrics.description: Great Britain (also known as 'Britain') is an island tucked between the North Sea and the English Channel, and is part of the British Isles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Great Britain' or 'Britain' to refer to the island (England, Scotland and Wales). Avoid using 'Britain' to mean the entire United Kingdom when Northern Ireland is involved—for example, saying 'Britain is leaving the E.U.' can be imprecise if you mean the U.K.

rubrics_metrics.name: England = one country within the U.K.
rubrics_metrics.description: England is one of the four countries that make up the U.K.; it is not synonymous with Britain or the United Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'England' when you mean the whole of Great Britain or the U.K. (common misusage). For example, avoid saying 'England voted to leave' if referring to the U.K. referendum result as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: British = ambiguous adjective
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'British' can refer to things that relate to the United Kingdom, Great Britain or the former British Empire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the ambiguity of 'British'—it may correctly describe something connected to the U.K. or to the broader historical empire. When precision matters, prefer the specific term (e.g., 'U.K.', 'Great Britain', 'England', 'British Overseas Territory').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved vs devolved matters within the U.K.
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the U.K., Parliament is sovereign, but each country has autonomy to some extent. Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish parliaments defer to the U.K. Parliament in 'reserved matters' like foreign policy and E.U. membership, but retain authority over 'devolved matters' like education and housing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing policy or constitutional questions (e.g., Brexit), distinguish whether the issue is a reserved matter (handled by U.K. Parliament) or a devolved matter (handled by the country’s own parliament/assembly). This distinction explains why different parts of the U.K. may have different policy control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republic of Ireland is a separate sovereign state
rubrics_metrics.description: Since becoming a republic in the 1940s, the Republic of Ireland has operated as a sovereign state of its own and has its own memberships with the United Nations, the E.U. and other international organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the Republic of Ireland with Northern Ireland or the U.K.; it is politically and legally separate. Be careful when discussing geographic proximity versus political status.

rubrics_metrics.name: British Overseas Territories remain under British rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The present-day U.K. does have a few remaining colonies worldwide, which are referred to as British Overseas Territories. These territories remain subject to British rule, though some are self-governing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When listing or referring to territories under British sovereignty, use the term 'British Overseas Territories' and be prepared to name examples (e.g., Anguilla, Bermuda, British Antarctic Territory, Falkland Islands, Gibraltar, Cayman Islands, Montserrat, Turks and Caicos, etc.). These are distinct from the U.K. proper and from Crown Dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crown Dependencies = self-governing possessions tied to the Crown
rubrics_metrics.description: Three islands within the British Isles retain special status as 'Crown Dependencies.' Though the U.K. is technically responsible for them, they are independently administered and self-governing. Instead of having a relationship with the U.K., they have a relationship with 'The Crown'—the British monarchy: Bailiwick of Jersey, Bailiwick of Guernsey, Isle of Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat Crown Dependencies as part of the U.K. proper; they are self-governing and constitutional ties are to the monarchy, not direct U.K. governance. Use their specific names when accuracy is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonwealth Realms accept the Crown but are independent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commonwealth Realm—countries that accept the Crown as their constitutional monarch—are members of the Commonwealth of Nations, each governs itself and makes its own domestic and foreign-policy decisions, but retain ties to the U.K. and to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing 'countries that share the Queen,' recognize they are independent sovereign states (examples: Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Jamaica, Papua New Guinea, etc.). Do not assume Commonwealth Realms are part of the U.K.; they simply share a monarch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and regional identity distinctions (example: Welsh)
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual countries within the U.K. retain their own local identities and even their own regional languages. Welsh, for example, is the official language in Wales even though the official language in the U.K., as a whole, is English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cultural and linguistic distinctions when referring to the constituent countries—language policy and identity differ across the nations of the U.K., and using the correct national/regional label shows accuracy and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating disparate international organizations or countries in commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Common gaffes include calling the E.U. the U.N. or lumping countries like Canada in with the U.K.’s exit from the E.U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check acronyms and memberships (E.U. vs U.N.) and do not assume other 'British-heritage' countries are politically tied to current U.K. membership decisions. Precision in naming prevents misleading statements (e.g., 'Britain leaving the E.U.' vs 'U.K. leaving the E.U.').
